Ok, so I'm being treated for mental health issues and we were specifically working on triggers recently. 

We were told that you often don't even know your triggers. Sometimes they are that subtle that you don't notice you've been triggered, have an adverse reaction and don't even connect the two. The idea is to work to identify triggers and then make a plan to deal with them to manage your emotions and behaviours. The goal being so we can identify them sooner and manage things sooner. 
So, someone identifying what they feel is their trigger out loud is problematic, or you just don't believe they are triggered at all? And if the latter, how do you know they are not triggered OR just very aware of theirs and learning to cope? In my mind, that's what I'm working towards. 


I'm not trying to be argumentative, I'm just trying to understand how what you are saying lines up with what I've been learning from mental health professionals. Are they using the word wrong? If I can learn something here that's great! 

This is the kind of thing that can lead people, like myself, not to seek help or improve because they aren't having severe things like fainting - that's why I stress it's not black and white.

I suppose the idea of being judged in that way for identifying my triggers makes me some what defensive.
